title: Idle tales (Luke 23:55–24:12)
hook: the women tell the apostles, and the words seem like idle tales

segments.voice: Yesterday, dikaios: at the cross a centurion said, indeed this was a just man. Your line was a just man.

Friday evening. The women from Galilee follow the body to the tomb and watch exactly where it's laid. They go home and prepare spices and ointments, and on the Sabbath, Luke says, they rest, according to the commandment. Saturday is long and silent. Very early on Sunday, in the half dark, they walk back carrying the spices, to do the last thing love can do for the dead. The stone is rolled back. The body is gone. And two men in shining clothes are standing there. Today, the first people to hear the news, and the first not to be believed.
screen: `THEY WATCH WHERE HE IS LAID.` → `A SILENT SABBATH.` → `SPICES AT DAWN, AN EMPTY TOMB.`

segments.voice: The two men ask the question that turns the whole Gospel: "Why seek you the living with the dead? He is not here, but is risen." Remember what he told you in Galilee. And they remembered his words. So the women go back and tell the eleven and all the rest. Luke names them: Mary Magdalen, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women with them. Here's how the news lands: "And these words seemed to them as idle tales; and they did not believe them." The Greek word is leros, and it's blunt: nonsense, silly talk, a word a medical writer of the time might use for the babbling of someone in a fever. The apostles, chosen and trained for three years, hear the first announcement of the resurrection and call it nonsense. Luke doesn't hide it. He could have. Peter does get up and run to the tomb. He stoops down, sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, and goes home wondering. Not believing yet. Wondering. The women had no body and no proof: an empty space, two strangers, and a memory. Earlier in Luke, when Jesus told the twelve what would happen in Jerusalem, they understood none of it. Now the women carry those same words back to them. The first people sent to say he is risen are the ones who came at dawn to anoint a corpse.
screen: `WHY SEEK THE LIVING WITH THE DEAD?` · `THE WOMEN REMEMBER, AND TELL.` · `LEROS: IT SOUNDED LIKE NONSENSE.` · `PETER RUNS, AND WONDERS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who told you something good lately and got a shrug back: a kid's story about their day, a friend saying things are finally getting better, a coworker excited about an idea you assumed wouldn't work. Picture their face, hear it again, and this time let it be true and be glad with them. If you pray, thank God for their news.
Idle tales. What the apostles called the women's report of the empty tomb. In Greek, leros: nonsense. They were wrong. Today's word.
Your line: not idle tales. The first news of the empty tomb came from the women. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's account of the empty tomb at the Easter Vigil in the year of Luke, the night the Alleluia returns after Lent.

original.note: Greek: nonsense, silly talk, Luke's word for how the women's report sounded (Luke 24:11).

trapdoor: what you thought: the apostles were the first to hear the resurrection.
what it means: the women heard first, remembered, and told, and the men dismissed it.
what a scholar hears: leros appears only here in the New Testament; Luke keeps an unflattering detail about the apostles in plain view.

chat.says: Who first heard that Jesus had risen, and did people believe them?
options: The women at the tomb; they told the apostles, who thought it idle tales.
Peter, who saw him at the tomb and told the women, who believed him.
The two men in shining clothes, who told the apostles, and all believed.
chat.meaning: Luke says the women brought the news from the empty tomb, and their words seemed to the apostles as idle tales.

Joanna.meaning: one of the women Luke names at the empty tomb

Mary Magdalen.meaning: a follower of Jesus who brought news from the tomb

Sabbath.meaning: the day of rest; the women rested then

notes: 'Leros' as a word medical writers used for delirious talk: commonly noted (e.g., in Hippocratic usage); confirm or soften.
'Leros appears only here in the New Testament': confirm.
'Apostle to the apostles' is attributed to Aquinas and earlier writers (e.g., Hippolytus' tradition, Rabanus Maurus); the 2016 decree uses the title. Confirm phrasing.
Luke 24:12 is absent from some Western manuscripts; the script tells it without comment. Confirm.
Confirm exact Douay wording of Luke 24:5–6 and 24:11.
